tagline: Doc platform that combines writing, tables, and small apps.
verdictSummary: A personal doc editor with embedded tables and simple formula columns is a real weekend build. What doesn't come with it is Coda's actual depth: a full formula language, a marketplace of integration 'packs,' team permissions, and the doc-as-app workflow that makes it a platform rather than an editor.
coreLoopDIY: A Markdown doc editor where a fenced block can embed a live table, with typed columns, simple formula columns, and buttons that run a small set of whitelisted actions.
whyPeopleStillPay: A doc that behaves like a small app is what teammates can actually understand and maintain without a developer — people pay for that workflow, not for tables inside a document.
notes: A useful sibling to Airtable in this catalogue, leaning more toward formulas and small workflows.
prompt:
Build a personal docs-with-tables tool: documents are Markdown, edited with a live preview, where a specially-marked fenced block references a table by name and renders it live inside the document. Tables have typed columns (text, number, date, select, checkbox) backed by a real database, with inline row editing. Support formula columns — a simple expression over a row's other fields, evaluated safely server-side with no imports and no network access, recomputed whenever a value changes. Let a document declare a button that runs one action from a small, fixed whitelist (add a row with defaults, mark a row done) — documents should never be able to execute arbitrary code. Support named, saved views per table (a filter plus a sort) that can be embedded in any document. Support CSV export per table and Markdown export per document.

Do not build real-time collaboration, permissions, or a packs and integrations ecosystem — Coda's formula language and pack marketplace are the actual product; this is a single-user personal version of the same idea, not a platform.

faq.q: Can I import my existing Coda docs?
faq.a: Coda exports documents and tables, and the table data maps reasonably well onto this build's schema. Formula columns don't transfer — Coda's formula language is proprietary, so each formula needs to be rewritten by hand.

faq.q: Will it work on my phone?
faq.a: For reading a doc, yes, as a responsive page. Editing tables and writing formulas is realistically a desktop task.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Hosting and a database, typically a few dollars a month, with no per-seat or per-doc pricing to think about.

faq.q: What's the one thing that doesn't survive the rebuild?
faq.a: The pack ecosystem. Coda's packs connect a doc to dozens of other tools with a few clicks; here, any integration with an outside service is code you write yourself, one at a time.
